extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of literary criticism; readers learning to analyze and judge poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reading, evaluating, and judging figurative language (metaphor, personification, tone, word-feeling relations) in poems, aimed at teaching close critical reading and sensible evaluative criteria. Focuses on how imagery, word choice, context and intent affect poetic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability/coherence of mixed imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: The mixture must not be of the fire and water type — which unfortunately is exactly what we have here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Images/elements combined in a poem must be compatible; incompatible mixtures damp or cancel the potency of each component. Evaluate whether components can coexist without neutralising each other's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of independent existence of images
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'higher potency in releasing vague emotion' that woven figurative language possesses is damped and cancelled as it blends with the sea and lightning ingredients, nor is there anything else in the passage that it can seek help from in preserving an independent existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that individual strands of imagery retain identifiable force within a compound figure; if one image is subsumed or obliterated by others, the emotional/evocative power may be lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification allowed if tied to a clear poetic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Personification...is a device which allows a poet to do almost anything he pleases with impunity provided, of course...he has anything worth doing in hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personification when it serves the poem's intention; it's permissible even for liberties in sense if the poet has a substantive aim that justifies it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification as condensation/economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Personification allows us to say compendiously and clearly what would be extraordinarily difficult to say without it...Condensation and economy are so often necessary in poetry — in order that emotional impulses shall not dissipate themselves — that all means to it are worth study. Personification...is perhaps the most important of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether personification contributes to economy and vividness (e.g., a single word conveying complex spatial/visual relations), and whether cutting it would make the sense cumbersome or less vivid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of personification and risk of overprojection
rubrics_metrics.description: There are degrees of personification; it can range from a mere momentary loan of a single human attribute or impulse to the projection of a complete spiritual being. Nothing recoils more heavily upon a poet than a too ample unjustified projection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the degree of personification and whether the poem can sustain it. Excessive or unjustified projection overloads the poem and destroys poetic sanction; delicate judgment is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of a clear conception of the personified object's personality
rubrics_metrics.description: 10.62 has not asked himself whether so shifting and various a thing as this cloud can be given a definite character, whether a changeful tricksiness is not all the personality it can bear. A 'clear conception' of the personality of the cloud would have hopelessly overburdened the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the poet has a coherent notion of the personified thing's character; if the object cannot plausibly bear a definite personality, the personification may be inappropriate or should be attenuated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge poetic means by irrelevant external standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The chemist must not require that the poet write like a chemist, nor the moralist, nor the man of affairs, nor the logician, that he write as they would...The aim of the poem comes first, and is the sole justification of its means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish the poem's intention before applying standards; avoid applying factual, logical, or professional criteria that are irrelevant to poetic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain the poem's intention before judging
rubrics_metrics.description: We may quarrel, frequently we must, with the aim of the poem, but we have first to ascertain what it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical judgment should begin with identifying the poem's aim (state of mind/intention) because that aim justifies the means. Misreading intention distorts evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative criticism fallacy — don't condemn difference as error
rubrics_metrics.description: What another poet did (here Shelley) in another poem is never in itself a good ground for deciding that this poet by doing differently has done wrong...This over-simple form of 'comparative criticism' is far too common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic comparison that presumes the prior example as normative. When comparing, compare intentions, conditions, and relevant methods, not superficial resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy, particularity and vividness as poetic virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The changed angle of incidence thus noted adds a solidness and particularity to the effect described, and since vividness is a large part of the intention of the poem at this point, the means employed should not be overlooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise concise, particular words/phrases that produce vivid visual or emotional effects; evaluate whether particularising language serves the poem's aims and emotional economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of mixing metaphors carelessly; check whether verbs/nouns align
rubrics_metrics.description: If 'hand' be read to mean a part of the cloud itself...the image becomes merely silly...Similarly with 'sidle'...gives the accidental, oblique quality...If read wrongly, the personification becomes silly and objections are explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test paraphrases and multiple readings to see if metaphors cohere syntactically and semantically; inappropriate readings often expose mixing or category errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader's sensitiveness and discrimination with words
rubrics_metrics.description: The enjoyment and understanding of the best poetry requires a sensitiveness and discrimination with words, a nicety, imaginativeness and deftness in taking their sense which will prevent Poem 9...from receiving the approval of the most attentive readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics/readers should cultivate fine discrimination in word-sense and nuance; failure of sensitivity can lead to rejecting subtle uses that are defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone as a central criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone, as a distinct character in a poem, is less easy to discuss than the others, and its importance may easily be overlooked...poetry...may sometimes take very high rank simply because the poet's attitude to his listeners...is so perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the poet's attitude toward the reader — appropriateness, manners, restraint vs over-insistence. Good tone can elevate commonplace thought; faults of tone (insulting, condescending, overdone) can ruin a poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners/proportion/historical code sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: We must distinguish between what may be called fundamental manners and the code that rules in any given period. Good manners for the eighteenth century may be atrocious by twentieth-century standards, or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tone/manners in light of both fundamental good manners (proportion) and period conventions; be historically informed when judging tone and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close reading required; poetry invites attention to literal sense to a point
rubrics_metrics.description: All respectable poetry invites close reading. It encourages attention to its literal sense up to the point, to be detected by the reader's discretion, at which liberty can serve the aim of the poem better than fidelity to fact or strict coherence among fictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage in careful literal-sense analysis before allowing figurative liberty; know when to stop literalism and allow liberties that serve poetic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of relation between sense and feeling (I, II, III)
rubrics_metrics.description: Type I: feeling generated by and governed by the sense. Type II: word first expresses a feeling, sense derived from the feeling. Type III: sense and feeling linked through context, less tightly knit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three types to analyse how words evoke feeling: decide whether feeling follows sense (I), feeling projects sense (II), or context mediates (III). This helps explain misreadings and how some words resist or yield to context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual pull: whether context integrates or warps a word's feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the pull exerted by the context...sufficient to overcome what may be described as the normal separate feeling of the questionable word? Can this pull bring it in, as an item either in accordance or in rude contrast to the rest? Or does the word resist, stay outside, or wrench the rest of the poem into crudity or confusion?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge if a word's customary feeling is assimilated by the poem's context or whether it jars; a resisting word may indicate a poet's power (if tamed) or a fault (if it wrecks the poem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulate emotional effect by examining sense-fabric of passage
rubrics_metrics.description: When a phrase strikes us as particularly happy, or particularly unfortunate, we can usually contrive, by examining the fabric of the sense into which it fits, to find rational grounds for our approval or dislike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how the phrase's sense interrelates with surrounding senses (implications, affinities, discrepancies) to account for its emotional effect rather than relying on gut reaction alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-awareness of critic's prejudices; practice cautious self-criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: My belief is that there every one is under the sway of preferences deeply rooted within, into the hands of which he unwittingly plays as he pursues his speculation...such self-criticism does not render obligatory any special tolerance of divergent opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of one's own biases and preferences when judging. Self-criticism tempers dogmatism, but does not require uncritical tolerance of opposing views that fail observational analysis.
